analysis.title: US Economic Weekly: Midterm mal(AI)se
key_insights: BofA's economists argue the midterm results raise the odds of more AI and data-center regulation, mostly at the state and local level. They expect it to slow the AI capex boom only marginally.

BofA says a bust in the AI investment cycle would come from demand and monetization, not regulation. Capex booms go bust when demand growth stops outpacing supply growth. For now demand indicators support aggressive capex plans.

Since the election, the S&P 500 is down 2.8%, the Nasdaq 100 is down 5.5% and the S&P 500 semiconductor and equipment index is down 14%. Before the election (Sep 1 to election day) the three were down 1.2%, 3.7% and 8.5%.

Exit polls show 56% of voters called AI and data centers a crucial or major factor in their congressional vote (23% crucial, 33% major). 76% oppose a data center in their community, and 40 of 41 ballot measures opposing data-center development passed.

Democrats won governor races in Texas, Ohio and Georgia. These three states hold 35% of data-center capacity under construction (by power) and 38% of planned capacity. BofA is watching how those governors shape data-center policy.

BofA's equity strategists (Savita Subramanian's team) project AI-related revenue growth will start to exceed AI-related capex growth as early as 3Q 2027. BofA says that supports the roughly 350GW of data-center capacity planned or under construction.

BofA says regulation like that enacted so far would raise costs without materially changing the economics. It may delay the point when AI revenue growth persistently outpaces capex growth. It does not expect regulation to affect the nearly 70GW of data-center power under construction.

BofA's utilities analyst Ross Fowler argues the results in Florida, Louisiana, North Dakota and Oklahoma are positive for the power and utilities sector. If Texas, Georgia or Ohio tighten rules, other states could benefit.

BofA still expects AI investment to add 30-50bp to US growth next year, and the growth impulse to stay intact for at least the next six to twelve months. Hyperscalers have not backed off capex plans, and 2027 capex expectations were revised higher again.

BofA sees only modest scope for tariff relief after the Democratic sweep. Tariffs brought in about $310bn over the last 12 months (nearly 1% of GDP) against a $2tn deficit. Likely beneficiaries are the EU, Canada, Mexico, Japan and Korea, which account for about a third of tariff revenue.

BofA's Oct CPI preview is 0.2% m/m for both headline and core, a bit softer than the prior two months. The BLS will not publish a y/y figure because October 2025 data were not collected during the shutdown. BofA initializes its Oct core PCE estimate at 0.2% m/m (0.22% unrounded, 3.2% y/y), which keeps a December hike firmly on the table.
BofA's 3Q GDP tracking rose 0.4pp to 3.8% q/q saar after construction spending, durable goods, factory orders and trade balance data. The advance 3Q GDP print was 3.4%.

BofA now expects two more Fed hikes at a quarterly pace, in Dec 2026 and Mar 2027, with a terminal rate of 4.25-4.5% held through end-2027. It sees two-sided risk: falling behind the curve, or stopping after one hike in December if y/y core PCE falls on favorable base effects.

Recent Fed commentary is hawkish. Logan wants at least two more 25bp hikes, Musalem says more firming is needed soon, and Collins and Williams see room for another hike. Barkin and Hammack favor a gradual path of smaller adjustments, and Bowman (Oct 14) saw no urgency to act.
BofA's card data show total card spending per household up 6.2% y/y in the week ending Oct 31, with gas up 25.0% y/y and department stores down 8.1%.

BofA's core views are 2.6% 4Q/4Q growth in 2026 and 2.1% in 2027, core PCE finishing 2026 slightly above 3% and falling to 2.5% in 2027, job growth averaging 70k a month in 2026 and about 60k in 2027-28, and the unemployment rate at 4.1% through 2027.

sector_views.rationale: Ross Fowler argues the midterm results in Florida, Louisiana, North Dakota and Oklahoma are positive for the sector, and states that avoid tighter rules could benefit if Texas, Georgia or Ohio tighten.
BofA expects regulation to slow the AI capex boom only marginally. Demand and monetization are the main risks, and AI revenue growth is not expected to outpace capex growth until about 3Q 2027.

earnings_insights: BofA's equity strategists note hyperscalers were penalized for any softness in results, and 2027 capex expectations were revised higher again.
The report cites a BofA Earnings Tracker (Week 3) noting plenty of beats, with Big Tech taking the heat. It gives no EPS or revenue figures.

tension_points.bull_case: BofA argues regulation will only marginally slow capex. Nearly 70GW of power under construction is unaffected, AI-related revenue growth should exceed capex growth by 3Q 2027, and hyperscalers keep raising 2027 capex.
tension_points.bear_case: Voters broadly oppose data centers (76% oppose local construction, 40 of 41 ballot measures passed), and Democrats won governor races in TX, OH and GA, which hold 35% of capacity under construction. Stricter rules raise costs and delay the point at which AI revenue growth exceeds capex growth.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Demand growth no longer outpacing supply growth, or AI monetization failing, would end the cycle. AI revenue growth failing to exceed capex growth by about 3Q 2027 would also undercut the case.

tension_points.bull_case: Strong growth, a balanced labor market and sticky inflation support two more hikes, in Dec 2026 and Mar 2027, taking the rate to 4.25-4.5%.
tension_points.bear_case: By moving slowly the Fed could fall behind the curve and have to hike more. Alternatively, y/y core PCE could roll off on favorable base effects early next year and the Fed stops after just one hike in December.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Y/y core PCE inflation rolling off due to favorable base effects early next year would leave the Fed stopping after one more hike in Dec 2026.

theme_stances.key_argument: Regulation is unlikely to stop the AI investment cycle, and demand and monetization matter more.
theme_stances.evidence: we do not think increased regulations are what stops the investment cycle

theme_stances.key_argument: Growth is solid, the labor market is balanced and inflation is too high, so two more hikes are coming at a quarterly pace.
theme_stances.evidence: we still expect two more hikes

theme_stances.key_argument: With a deficit of $2tn the government can't afford to lose much tariff revenue.
theme_stances.evidence: We see only modest scope for tariff relief
